triage.reason: Common metabolic bone disease; case built on fracture risk history, DEXA interpretation and secondary causes, though often asymptomatic until fracture.

chief_complaints.text: I broke my wrist after a small fall
I've gotten shorter over the past few years
My back has started to hurt
My doctor said my bone scan was low
I don't have any symptoms — my doctor just wants to check my bones

hpi.onset: Usually gradual and silent over years; often first noticed when a fracture occurs or on routine screening
hpi.duration: Chronic, developing over years to decades
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive bone loss; may remain asymptomatic until a fragility fracture, height loss or stooped posture develops
hpi.location: Most fractures occur at the hip, spine (vertebral bodies) and wrist; height loss and back pain reflect the spine
hpi.radiation: Back pain from a vertebral fracture may radiate around the trunk or to the flank
hpi.quality: No pain at baseline; fracture pain is sharp and localized, while vertebral compression pain is deep and aching
hpi.severity: Asymptomatic until fracture; fracture pain can be moderate to severe
hpi.timing: Fractures often follow minor trauma or a fall from standing height; back pain may be acute after a vertebral fracture or chronic from multiple fractures

associated_symptoms.text: Fracture after minor trauma or fall from standing height
Decreased grip strength or difficulty with daily activities
Loss of appetite or weight loss

pertinent_negatives: Bone pain at rest unrelated to fracture

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with a fragility fracture after a fall, or with height loss and kyphosis; often asymptomatic until a fracture occurs.
Osteoporosis in children is rare and usually secondary to another condition or medication; presents with fractures or bone pain rather than screening findings.
Transient osteoporosis of pregnancy can cause hip pain and fractures, but it is a distinct, usually self-limited condition.
Chronic kidney disease can cause renal osteodystrophy with bone pain and fractures, and osteoporosis may coexist.
Type 1 diabetes is associated with lower bone density and increased fracture risk, often at a younger age.
Higher body weight is generally protective for bone density, but obesity does not eliminate fracture risk, especially with falls.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; normal posture and gait
general.moderate: Well-appearing but with mild thoracic kyphosis or a measured height loss; steady gait
general.severe: Stooped posture with prominent thoracic kyphosis (dowager's hump); may use a cane or walk slowly
general.critical: Fracture-related pain limiting movement; may be unable to bear weight or stand from a chair without help

criteria.name: World Health Organization DXA criteria
criteria.summary: Osteoporosis is defined by a T-score at or below -2.5 at the lumbar spine, femoral neck or total hip. A T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 is low bone mass (osteopenia). A fragility fracture of the hip or spine establishes the diagnosis regardless of T-score.
items: T-score at or below -2.5 at the lumbar spine, femoral neck or total hip
T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 indicates low bone mass
Fragility fracture of the hip or spine confirms osteoporosis regardless of T-score

differential.name: Osteomalacia
differential.why_considered: Both cause low bone density, fractures and bone pain in older adults, and both can follow vitamin D deficiency or malabsorption.
differential.trigger: Diffuse bone pain, muscle weakness, or low calcium and phosphorus with a high alkaline phosphatase

history: Diffuse aching bone pain and muscle weakness, especially in the hips and thighs
Difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs
Poor dietary vitamin D or calcium, or malabsorption
Little or no history of fragility fracture
exam: Proximal muscle weakness and a waddling gait
Bone tenderness on pressure over the long bones or pelvis
No kyphosis or height loss early in the course
labs: Low or low-normal calcium and phosphorus
Elevated PTH secondary to vitamin D deficiency
imaging: Looser zones (pseudofractures) on x-ray
Diffuse osteopenia on DXA without the typical postmenopausal pattern

differential.name: Multiple myeloma
differential.why_considered: Causes lytic bone lesions, bone pain and fractures in older adults, and can be mistaken for osteoporosis when the patient presents with a fragility fracture.
differential.trigger: Bone pain at rest, anemia, hypercalcemia, or a markedly elevated ESR with fractures

history: Persistent bone pain, often in the back or ribs, worse at night
exam: Point tenderness over the ribs or spine
No kyphosis or height loss out of proportion to age
labs: Elevated total protein with a monoclonal spike on serum protein electrophoresis
imaging: Punched-out lytic lesions on skeletal survey or low-dose whole-body CT
Vertebral compression fractures without generalized osteopenia

differential.name: Hyperparathyroidism
differential.why_considered: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes bone loss, especially at the cortical bone of the distal radius, and is a reversible secondary cause of osteoporosis.

exam: Usually normal; may have band keratopathy or a palpable neck mass
imaging: Subperiosteal bone resorption of the radial aspects of the middle phalanges
Salt-and-pepper appearance of the skull
Brown tumors in severe cases

differential.name: Hyperthyroidism
differential.why_considered: Thyroid hormone excess accelerates bone turnover and causes bone loss, and is a reversible cause of osteoporosis.

history: Heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss despite increased appetite
labs: Low TSH with elevated free T4 or T3
Elevated alkaline phosphatase from increased bone turnover
imaging: Diffuse or nodular goiter on thyroid ultrasound
Increased uptake on radioactive iodine scan

differential.name: Cushing syndrome
differential.why_considered: Glucocorticoid excess, whether endogenous or from steroid therapy, is a strong cause of bone loss and fractures.

history: Weight gain around the trunk with thinning of the arms and legs
exam: Moon facies, buffalo hump, truncal obesity
imaging: Adrenal nodule or hyperplasia on CT
Pituitary adenoma on MRI

differential.name: Metastatic bone disease
differential.why_considered: Bone metastases from breast, prostate, lung, kidney or thyroid cancer cause fractures and bone pain in older adults and can mimic osteoporosis.
differential.trigger: Bone pain at rest, weight loss, or a fracture with an atypical pattern or location

history: Known primary cancer or weight loss
Bone pain that is constant and worse at night
Fracture after minimal trauma at an unusual site
labs: Elevated tumor markers if the primary is known
imaging: Lytic or blastic lesions on x-ray, often in the axial skeleton
Multiple lesions on bone scan or PET
MRI showing marrow replacement

differential.name: Paget disease of bone
differential.why_considered: Causes bone pain, deformity and fractures in older adults, and can be confused with osteoporosis when the spine or hip is involved.

history: Bone pain that is deep and aching, often in the pelvis, femur or skull
exam: Bone deformity or bowing of the legs
labs: Markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphorus
imaging: Coarse trabecular thickening and cortical thickening on x-ray
Cotton-wool appearance of the skull
Increased uptake on bone scan

differential.name: Renal osteodystrophy
differential.why_considered: Chronic kidney disease causes bone loss, bone pain and fractures through disordered mineral metabolism, and often coexists with osteoporosis.

history: Known chronic kidney disease or dialysis
imaging: Rugger jersey spine on x-ray
Subperiosteal bone resorption
Vascular calcification

severity.mild: Low bone mass (osteopenia) or a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 without a fragility fracture; no symptoms and no height loss.
severity.moderate: Osteoporosis by T-score at or below -2.5 without a fragility fracture, or a single mild vertebral compression fracture with mild back pain and early height loss.
severity.severe: Established osteoporosis with one or more fragility fractures, height loss of 2 cm or more, thoracic kyphosis, chronic back pain and reduced mobility.
severity.critical: Fragility fracture of the hip or multiple vertebral fractures with severe pain, immobility, and risk of complications such as pneumonia, venous thromboembolism or pressure ulcers.

red_flags.meaning: Acute vertebral compression fracture; needs imaging and pain control

red_flags.finding: Inability to bear weight or stand after a fall
red_flags.meaning: Possible hip fracture; requires urgent orthopedic evaluation

red_flags.finding: New leg weakness, numbness, or bowel or bladder dysfunction
red_flags.meaning: Possible spinal cord or cauda equina compression from a fracture; emergency

red_flags.finding: Bone pain at rest, weight loss, or a fracture at an unusual site
red_flags.meaning: Suggests malignancy such as multiple myeloma or metastatic disease rather than primary osteoporosis
Points toward hyperparathyroidism or malignancy as the cause of bone loss

special_populations.differences: Highest fracture risk; falls are common and often multifactorial. Screen with DXA and fall risk assessment, and treat to reduce fracture risk.
Transient osteoporosis of pregnancy can cause hip pain and fractures, but it is usually self-limited. DXA is not routinely used during pregnancy.
Chronic kidney disease causes renal osteodystrophy and alters mineral metabolism. Check renal function before bisphosphonates and consider nephrology input.
Type 1 diabetes is associated with lower bone density and increased fracture risk at a younger age. Type 2 diabetes may have normal or high bone density but still increased fracture risk.
Higher body weight is generally protective for bone density, but obesity does not eliminate fracture risk, especially with falls.
Osteoporosis in children is rare and usually secondary to another condition or medication. Presents with fractures or bone pain rather than screening findings.

key_questions.question: Have you ever broken a bone, and if so, how did it happen?
key_questions.looking_for: A fragility fracture — a break from a fall at standing height or less, or with minimal trauma — especially of the hip, spine or wrist after age 50

key_questions.question: Have you noticed that you are getting shorter, or that your posture has changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Height loss of 2 cm or more, or increasing thoracic kyphosis, suggesting vertebral compression fractures

key_questions.question: Do you have back pain, and if so, when did it start and what were you doing?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute midline back pain after bending, lifting or a minor fall suggests a vertebral compression fracture; chronic pain suggests multiple fractures

key_questions.question: Have you fallen recently, or do you feel unsteady on your feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Falls or balance problems, which drive fracture risk and are a target for prevention

key_questions.question: When did your periods stop, and did you have your ovaries removed?
key_questions.looking_for: Early menopause or bilateral oophorectomy, which accelerates bone loss through estrogen deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you taken steroid medicines such as prednisone, or acid-reducing medicines, for a long time?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-term glucocorticoids (strongest drug cause), proton pump inhibitors, antiseizure medicines, heparin or medroxyprogesterone

key_questions.question: Has a parent had osteoporosis or broken a hip?
key_questions.looking_for: Parental history of osteoporosis or hip fracture, a strong independent risk factor

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or drink alcohol, and how much?
key_questions.looking_for: Current smoking and heavy alcohol use, both modifiable risks for bone loss and falls

key_questions.question: How much calcium and vitamin D do you get in your diet, and do you take supplements?
key_questions.looking_for: Low dietary calcium or vitamin D intake, which contributes to bone loss and is correctable

key_questions.question: How much do you exercise, and have you been on bedrest or inactive for long periods?
key_questions.looking_for: Sedentary lifestyle or prolonged immobilization, which accelerates bone loss

key_questions.question: Have you had thyroid, parathyroid, kidney, liver or intestinal problems, or an eating disorder?
key_questions.looking_for: Secondary causes such as hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, rheumatoid arthritis or anorexia nervosa

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying, or had fevers or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms that raise concern for malignancy such as multiple myeloma or metastatic disease rather than primary osteoporosis

key_questions.question: Do you have any pain at rest in your bones, or pain that wakes you at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Constant or nocturnal bone pain suggests malignancy or infection rather than osteoporosis

key_questions.question: Have you ever had kidney stones, or any numbness, weakness or trouble with bowel or bladder control?
key_questions.looking_for: Kidney stones suggest hyperparathyroidism; neurologic or bowel/bladder symptoms suggest spinal cord compression from a fracture

reasoning_points: The patient is a postmenopausal woman over age 50, the most typical demographic for primary osteoporosis
A fragility fracture after a fall from standing height or less is the hallmark presentation and can establish the diagnosis
Height loss, thoracic kyphosis or acute midline back pain suggest vertebral compression fractures
The disease is usually silent until a fracture, so screening history and DXA are central
Risk factors include advanced age, estrogen deficiency, low body weight, smoking, heavy alcohol use, low calcium and vitamin D intake, and physical inactivity
Long-term glucocorticoid use is the strongest medication-related cause and should be specifically asked about

Secondary causes must be excluded before calling it primary osteoporosis: hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, Cushing syndrome and multiple myeloma
The diagnosis is confirmed by a DXA T-score at or below -2.5 at the lumbar spine, femoral neck or total hip, or by a fragility fracture of the hip or spine
A T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 indicates low bone mass (osteopenia), not osteoporosis
Red flags such as bone pain at rest, weight loss, anemia or hypercalcemia should prompt evaluation for malignancy rather than primary osteoporosis
Fall risk assessment and fracture risk assessment guide treatment decisions
